audience: A student with first-course linear algebra and single-variable calculus; no prior probability course assumed.
review_scope: Read the immutable full page teaching context, application model, relevant walkthrough and flashcards; read every baseline exercise, question, hint and original solution alongside its selected draft solution.

Independently assessed all calculations, logical steps, theorem hypotheses, notation, uncertainty, interpretation and every requested subpart. Straightforward readiness answers were not expanded merely for length.

Derived elementary results directly and applied the precisely stated chapter theorems when suitable; the optional uniform-MGF refinement and conformal conditional-coverage formulas are worked through at the prerequisite level.
Computed selected solution SHA256 values from the actual candidate and verified exact agreement with each draft selection and original baseline hash.

Independently recomputed numerical values with exact rational arithmetic and elementary formulas; normal CDF/tails use erfc and quantiles use Python statistics.NormalDist. The author numeric helper was not invoked.
Verified that the integrated and authoring candidates preserve every byte outside their original solution slots, including questions, hints, summaries, anchors and scripts.

exercises.label: Exercise C.R1 — Readiness: Translate a complement
exercises.reasoning: Retain is justified for this one-step readiness problem. The complement partitions the sample space with A, so 1-0.15=0.85; the text identifies no violation with A^c and states the scope of that event. Both questions are answered without unnecessary expansion.

exercises.label: Exercise C.R2 — Readiness: Build a weighted average
exercises.reasoning: Retain is justified. The four representative values give (2+6+6+6)/4=5, and the equivalent probability-weighted expression is shown. The solution explains why 2+6 ignores frequencies and normalization. This is enough detail for the requested elementary average.

exercises.label: Exercise C.R3 — Readiness: Check an outer product
exercises.reasoning: The replacement shows every matrix entry in vv^T, expands the arbitrary quadratic form to w_1^2+4w_1w_2+4w_2^2, and factors it as a square. The nonnegative result proves PSD for every w; the nonzero zero direction correctly distinguishes PD. Both requested operations are fully explained.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S1 — Easy: Read a probability table
exercises.reasoning: The solution checks nonnegative masses and their sum, identifies the two disjoint outcomes in X>=2, and weights each cost to obtain E[X]=3/2. It answers all three requests and explains why an average need not be a possible outcome. The expansion makes each probability-table operation visible.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S2 — Medium: Variance is an average of squared distances
exercises.reasoning: All requested quantities are computed: E[X^2]=5, Var(X)=11/4, SD=sqrt(11)/2, E[3X+1]=11/2 and Var(3X+1)=99/4. The centered-difference identity explains why the shift cancels and the variance scale is 9. The second moment and fraction arithmetic are explicit.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S3 — Hard: A covariance calculation that detects dependence
exercises.reasoning: The three equally weighted outcomes supply both means, the cross moment, and both variances, giving diag(2/3,2/9). Dependence is proved with P(X=0|Y=0)=1 versus P(X=0)=1/3, so zero covariance is not mistaken for independence. Every covariance-matrix entry and the conceptual part are covered.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S4 — Easy: Restrict and renormalise
exercises.reasoning: Events A, B and A intersect B are listed before their probabilities are calculated. Dividing 2/6 by the positive 3/6 gives 2/3; the equivalent two-out-of-three argument explains renormalization. All unconditional and conditional requests are answered.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S5 — Medium: Bayes by counting imaginary runs
exercises.reasoning: The table accounts for all 1000 hypothetical runs, including 80 true and 180 false alarms. Total probability gives 0.26 and conditioning gives 4/13. The answer explains the reversed conditional and the base-rate effect, and labels the counts as an illustration of the assumed law.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S6 — Hard: Separate noise from disagreement
exercises.reasoning: The mean is 2 and total variance is within-model 1 plus between-model 4. The centered decomposition and zero conditional mean justify the vanished cross term. The second-moment check gives 9-4=5 and confirms that no Gaussian assumption is used.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S7 — Easy: Advance a distribution one step
exercises.reasoning: The row-vector convention, initial law, and both matrix transitions are shown. The two-step path sums give (0.70,0.30) and normalization is checked. The explanation correctly uses conditional transition products instead of independence of consecutive states.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S8 — Medium: Solve a stationary distribution
exercises.reasoning: The stationary first-coordinate equation is expanded to 0.5a=0.3, giving (0.6,0.4), and the other coordinate is checked. The unchanged law is explicitly distinguished from individual paths that continue to switch. Both algebra and interpretation are complete.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S9 — Hard: Why copying data does not increase sample size
exercises.reasoning: The two recorded averages are expressed using their actual independent draws. Independence gives variance 0.16/100=0.0016 for the first and 0.16/50=0.0032 for the duplicated experiment. Standard deviations and unbiasedness are compared, and copying is correctly identified as dependence rather than extra information.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S10 — Easy: Variance is not standard deviation
exercises.reasoning: The answer identifies variance 4 and SD 2, standardizes both thresholds, and uses symmetry for the central interval. It gives 0.8413 and 0.6826 using the supplied rounded Phi(1), and correctly interprets the one-SD interval. No requested part is omitted.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S11 — Medium: One noisy measurement
exercises.reasoning: The Gaussian prior-likelihood product is written, expanded and completed to (5/4)(f-12/5)^2+9/5. The posterior mean 12/5 and variance 4/5 follow from the exponent, and an independent future noise adds 1 for predictive variance 9/5. The latent/predictive distinction and conditional scope are clear.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S12 — Hard: A chance constraint along a direction
exercises.reasoning: Joint Gaussianity justifies the scalar Gaussian projection. Both covariance cross terms are included, giving mean 3 and variance 6. Strict monotonicity of Phi derives the exact minimum b=3+sqrt(6)Phi^{-1}(0.95). The supplied quantile is correctly treated as an estimate below the exact threshold, preserving the guarantee.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S13 — Easy: An upper bound can be loose
exercises.reasoning: Markov is justified from nonnegativity and the event lower bound on X. Threshold 8 gives 1/4, while threshold 1 yields the true but uninformative bound 2, clipped to the probability bound 1. Both queries and the difference between a bound and an estimate are explained.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S14 — Medium: Plan a Hoeffding sample size
exercises.reasoning: The independent [0,1] assumptions justify two-sided Hoeffding. The logarithm and negative-division steps give N>=ln(40)/0.02, so the sufficient integer is 185. Checking the adjacent integers verifies upward rounding. The answer does not claim that this sufficient bound is a universal minimum sample size.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S15 — Hard: A bounded bias survives averaging
exercises.reasoning: The mean bias 1 is identified and an explicit uniform-density integral violates the proposed R=2 MGF bound at lambda=1/4. Centering gives xi=epsilon-1 in [-1,1] with zero mean and Hoeffding parameter 1. The corrected observation model retains the bias, answering both mathematical and modeling parts.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S16 — Easy: One statement or all statements?
exercises.reasoning: The complement of all passes is the union of failures. Adding the three upper failure probabilities gives simultaneous success at least 0.97 under arbitrary dependence. The independent product is correctly presented only as an extra-assumption lower bound. All requested reasoning is supplied.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S17 — Medium: A finite grid of confidence intervals
exercises.reasoning: Ten equal budgets of 0.005 are assigned and each within-data-set Hoeffding bound is solved, giving N>=ln(400)/0.02 and N=300. The union budget proves at least 0.95 simultaneous confidence, and the answer separates within-set independence from arbitrary dependence across sets.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S18 — Hard: Guarantees at every time
exercises.reasoning: The finite reciprocal sum is expanded and telescoped to 0.05(1-1/(T+1)). Its limit and the increasing union give any-time failure at most 0.05. Constant budgets are correctly rejected as a justification, and independent 0.05 failures provide a concrete counterexample with no-failure probability 0.95^T tending to zero.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S19 — Easy: A fair random walk
exercises.reasoning: The next sum is split into the known S_t and the independent fair sign. Its conditional expectation is explicitly zero, giving E[S_{t+1}|F_t]=S_t. Adaptedness and integrability follow from the past and |S_t|<=t. The martingale conditions and the absence of conditional drift are explained.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S20 — Medium: An adaptive multiplier can preserve zero drift
exercises.reasoning: The multiplier is selected before the new sign and is known given F_{t-1}; taking it outside conditioning is therefore valid. Given the past, D_t is centered in [-a_t,a_t], and the displayed MGF inequalities certify local a_t and uniform R=2. The answer correctly allows adaptive dependence.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S21 — Hard: Looking ahead breaks the argument
exercises.reasoning: Enumerating both signs shows D_t=epsilon_t^2=1, so its conditional mean is 1 and its accumulated sum is deterministic T. The failed pull-out step is precisely identified as lacking past measurability. This directly addresses the claim and explains why fairness is lost after the look-ahead transformation.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S22 — Easy: Entropy of a fair and a biased coin
exercises.reasoning: Both outcome contributions appear in each entropy. The exact expressions give ln(2)=0.693147 and H(1/4)=0.562335 nats; the bias interpretation and logarithm units are supplied. Intermediate decimal contributions are explicitly rounded evaluations, and both requested laws are covered.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S23 — Medium: Total variation and directional KL
exercises.reasoning: TV is computed symmetrically as 0.25. The ratios and first-law weights are shown separately in each KL direction, giving 0.130812 and 0.143841 nats. The differing results explain direction dependence. All three requested quantities are correctly evaluated.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S24 — Hard: Support mismatch and a useless KL bound
exercises.reasoning: The zero-weight convention yields KL(p||q)=ln(2), while positive q mass against zero p mass yields infinite reverse KL. TV is 0.5 and Pinsker from the finite direction gives sqrt(ln(2)/2)=0.588705. The solution explains why the infinite direction supplies no useful bound.

independent_calculations.KL_q_p: infinite: positive mass over zero reference mass

exercises.label: Exercise C.S25 — Easy: Find the first threshold reaching the target
exercises.reasoning: The piecewise CDF includes equality at each atom. Applying the infimum definition gives VaR_0.8=0 and VaR_0.9=VaR_0.95=10. The residual 0.05 mass above 10 is stated, explaining the equality convention and preventing a worst-case interpretation.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S26 — Medium: Take the worst ten percent, including part of an atom
exercises.reasoning: The worst 0.1 mass selects all 0.05 at 100 and 0.05 of the 0.15 atom at 10, giving CVaR=55. The full mean is 6.5 and conditional tail mean is 32.5 because it uses 0.2 mass. The answer explains fractional selection of the atom and covers the requested comparison.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S27 — Hard: Verify the optimisation formula at a kink
exercises.reasoning: The positive-part expectation is expanded and each interval yields a full affine expression: 65-9nu, 65-nu, 50+0.5nu and nu. These give slopes -9,-1,0.5,1. Continuity plus the sign change locates the minimum at 10, and direct substitution gives 55 despite the nondifferentiable kink.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S28 — Easy: Exactly two failures
exercises.reasoning: The probability of a specified failing pair is computed using independence, then the six disjoint pair patterns are added to give 0.0486. The no-failure complement gives 0.3439 for at least one failure. The explanation keeps product independence and disjoint addition distinct.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S29 — Medium: Zero failures still leaves uncertainty
exercises.reasoning: The root equation is solved to p_U=1-0.05^{1/100}=0.029513, with the positive root justified. The monotone data probability is interpreted as test inversion, and the at-least-95% statement applies to a repeated-data procedure for fixed p. It does not turn the bound into a posterior or infer p=0.

exercises.label: Exercise C.S30 — Hard: Ranks, ties and marginal coverage
exercises.reasoning: Exchangeability with distinct scores gives each of the 20 ranks probability 1/20. The comparison with the 18th calibration score is proved in both directions, yielding acceptance 18/20=0.9. The subgroup average example explains why marginal coverage does not establish subgroup or fixed-calibration-set coverage; ties are explicitly outside this argument.

exercises.label: Exercise C.B1 — Easy: A new production line changes the inspection decision
exercises.reasoning: All rates and the decision costs are restored from the application context. The two alarm routes give 0.0882 and posterior 5/49, so conditional release loss 150/49 is below inspection cost 6. Silence is also checked. Whole-rule costs 0.30 versus 0.5592 complete the comparison under perfect inspection and the stated model.

exercises.label: Exercise C.B2 — Medium: Offset uncertainty is not reading uncertainty
exercises.reasoning: The solution conditions on the calibrated posterior mean 7/6 mm and variance 2/3 mm^2. Fresh independent Gaussian noise gives total reading-error variance 5/3 mm^2 and coverage 0.87866 within 2 mm, below 0.98. It clearly distinguishes offset-only coverage from predictive reading coverage and retains units.

exercises.label: Exercise C.B3 — Hard: Repeated use shares the same uncertain offset
exercises.reasoning: The shared offset U remains once in the average, while the n fresh noises average to variance 1/n. This gives 203/300 mm^2 at 100 readings and limiting 2/3 mm^2. The cross-covariance 2/3 between different errors explains why (5/3)/100 is invalid. The fixed correction and conditional model are stated.

exercises.label: Exercise C.B4 — Hard: Plan a batch reliability requirement
exercises.reasoning: The batch event is defined as a union, yielding sufficient q<=0.0004 under arbitrary dependence. Independent equal rates give exact q<=1-0.98^{1/50}=0.000403973 via an order-preserving root. The example 0.004 fails both allowances, with independent batch failure 0.18160; assumed rates are not presented as data confidence bounds.

exercises.label: Exercise C.1 — Monte Carlo estimates and zero failures
exercises.reasoning: Parts (a)-(c) are explicitly answered. Bernoulli indicators give estimate 0.07 and plug-in SE 0.0180416; the approximate normal interval is [0.0346384,0.1053616]. Zero failures expose the boundary failure of that plug-in estimate, and test inversion gives exact one-sided p_U=1-0.05^{1/200}=0.014867. Frequentist and posterior interpretations remain distinct.

exercises.label: Exercise C.2 — An alarm, a base rate and many steps
exercises.reasoning: All three parts restore their relevant event and assumptions. Bayes gives change-after-alarm 90/139; expectation gives 5 false alarms and independence gives any-alarm probability 0.99343. An equal union budget gives per-step 0.0001 and exact two-sided Gaussian threshold Phi^{-1}(0.99995)=3.890591886. The conservative 3.89060 avoids rounding below the guarantee.

exercises.label: Exercise C.3 — A Gaussian posterior and a safety probability
exercises.reasoning: Precision of the sample mean is 16, so posterior precision 17 gives m=72/85 and s^2=1/17. The 0.5 threshold is standardized to probability 0.07622. The lower bound is 0.361988>0.3, and its failure is the one-sided posterior tail Phi(-2)=0.02275. The answer explicitly distinguishes bound failure from the event f<0.3 and addresses all parts.

exercises.label: Exercise C.4 — How many runs, and which $R$?
exercises.reasoning: The solution derives the worst-case [0,1] variance bound from X^2<=X before using independence. Chebyshev and Hoeffding give sufficient sizes 10000 and 1060. Uniform-noise range and SD give R=0.2 and sigma=0.2/sqrt(3). The optional sharper R claim is proved through MGF coefficients and second-order necessity, and the shifted-noise bias 0.1 is modeled separately. All three parts are complete at the stated calculus level.

exercises.label: Exercise C.5 — KL, total variation and Pinsker
exercises.reasoning: Each KL sum uses the correct first-law weights, giving 0.0876597 and 0.0915162, with TV 0.2. Both Pinsker bounds are evaluated and checked. The support mismatch with q-prime makes only KL(p||q-prime) infinite; the reverse finite expression and its consequence for a new-to-old trust-region constraint are explained. All parts are covered.

exercises.label: Exercise C.6 — VaR, CVaR and the Gaussian shortcut
exercises.reasoning: The discrete mean, violation probability, VaR and atom-split CVaR are derived; the Rockafellar-Uryasev calculation independently gives the same 6. Second moment 5.6 yields variance 4.96. The Gaussian upper-tail integral is explained using phi-prime=-w phi, giving comparison CVaR 4.70853. The final three constraint decisions are tied to the actual law, showing why the Gaussian approximation would wrongly accept the CVaR constraint.

exercises.label: Exercise C.7 — Conformal coverage is itself random
exercises.reasoning: Every requested part is derived. The rank threshold is 18 with marginal coverage 0.9. The uniform order-statistic CDF is counted and differentiated to the Beta(18,2) density, and elementary integrals give E[C]=9/10, E[C^2]=57/70, Var(C)=3/700, SD=0.0654654 and P(C<0.8)=0.0828662. Conditional binomial test variance and total variance give 303/70000 and SD=0.0657919. The calibration contribution dominates, and i.i.d. continuity is distinguished from exchangeability alone.
